title: Hookback
user: Self-taught instrumentalists who want to learn melodies by ear from songs they already like, rather than drill abstract intervals.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The 128-comment ear-training discussion asks for examples before tests; several musicians say clinical interval drills do not transfer to playing freely and recommend familiar melodic hooks and singing.
A web-music maker reports that an attempted early note leaves sampler readiness invisible even though notes later play, illustrating the fragile feedback loop in browser practice tools.

recurrence: One large, multi-asker 2026 thread plus a separate browser-audio failure report; motivation and reliable immediate feedback are both high-severity for daily practice.
current_workaround: Loop a song in YouTube/Spotify, slow it manually, then check notes against a piano or a generic interval quiz.
incumbents_and_gap: ToneDear, Perfect Ear, and musictheory.net offer excellent drills, but do not turn a user-selected 5–12 second local clip into a private listen-sing/play-compare loop with an achievable next hint.
smallest_useful_product: PWA that accepts a local audio clip, loops an A/B region, records a short microphone or MIDI answer, estimates contour/pitch distance, and keeps a lightweight practice queue. Non-goals: streaming-catalog import, transcription of full songs, social feed, or AI song generation.
success_measure: 40% of activated users complete three clip-response loops on three separate days, and 60% rate the feedback as more useful than an interval-only drill.
monetization: freemium — the local core should remain free; a paid tier can add saved practice packs and advanced progress review without selling user audio.
constraints: Process clips and microphone audio locally by default; do not redistribute copyrighted recordings; show a clear recording indicator and support MIDI without write access.
why_distinct: It teaches transferable musical recall from the learner's own short clips, not another question-bank ear trainer or an LLM music generator.

title: MIDI First Note
user: Piano teachers and hobbyists using browser exercises who need a five-minute, no-account way to verify that a MIDI keyboard, browser permissions, sound, and note mapping all work before a lesson.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker releases a MIDI-based piano trainer, demonstrating continuing demand for browser-based instrument practice rather than installation-heavy software.
In the discussion of a web drum machine, a commenter says drum machines are fun regardless of skill level, reinforcing the value of immediate, low-friction instrument access.

recurrence: Independent music-tool communities in 2025–26 continue to build and try browser MIDI instruments; setup failure happens before the lesson can begin.
current_workaround: Open a lesson site, guess which browser/device setting failed, install a DAW, or ask a teacher to troubleshoot live.
incumbents_and_gap: Chrome's MIDI indicators, DAWs, and individual lesson apps expose pieces of the stack; none produces a shareable, privacy-safe readiness card covering input, pitch map, latency, sustain, and audio unlock.
smallest_useful_product: A static web app that detects MIDI ports, plays/labels the received notes, measures round-trip tap timing, checks sustain/pitch-bend, and exports a redacted support card. Non-goals: sequencer, notation editor, or cloud account.
success_measure: 80% of first-time users obtain a green input-and-audio card in under three minutes; teachers report fewer than one setup interruption per five remote lessons.
monetization: free — it is an adoption utility for lesson authors; optional branded embed/support analytics could be paid later.
constraints: Request only MIDI access needed for input; never retain device names or played notes unless the user downloads the card; disclose browser/platform limitations.
why_distinct: The unit of value is a comprehensible setup diagnosis, not a piano-learning course or virtual instrument.

title: Shot Runner
user: Small animation teams and technical artists who need repeatable preview renders for named shots without driving a browser UI or maintaining a full studio pipeline.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Discussion of a new 2D animation tool asks for real production workflows, color management, and actual animation tools rather than a browser-tech demo.
A user explicitly requests a documented CLI to render animations headlessly for an automated server pipeline, with no GUI or manual browser interaction.

recurrence: A production-workflow critique and an explicit automated-render request point to the same costly handoff: a shot is ready but previews are manual and non-repeatable.
current_workaround: Keep a browser or editor open, click export per shot, record ad-hoc shell notes, or build a bespoke render script.
incumbents_and_gap: After Effects render queues and full render farms are broad; Motion Canvas is code-first. Small teams lack a tiny manifest-driven layer that can run heterogeneous local render commands and preserve the preview receipt.
smallest_useful_product: Local CLI reading a shot manifest, invoking allowlisted renderer commands, caching frame sequences, producing contact sheets and a JSON receipt with source hash/fps/colorspace. Non-goals: animation authoring, cloud rendering, video hosting, or generative video.
success_measure: A pilot renders five named shots from one command and can reproduce a selected preview bit-for-bit after a clean checkout.
monetization: one-time — episodic local-pipeline value suits a durable desktop/CLI license better than render-minute billing.
constraints: Never execute commands from untrusted manifests without confirmation; clearly surface renderer licensing and local ffmpeg requirements; store no media remotely.
why_distinct: It is a provenance and repeatability layer around existing creative tools, not another timeline editor.

title: Export Proof
user: People publishing diagrams, collaborative pixel canvases, and teaching visuals who need confidence that a PNG/PDF export says the same thing as the live canvas.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Show HN post introduces a persistent collaborative pixel canvas, a use case where a shareable static export is part of the creative artifact.
A report shows labels that are correct on the interactive canvas but wrap and are clipped in the PNG export, making the exported diagram unreadable.

recurrence: A live-canvas product and a concrete export mismatch show a recurring last-mile failure: the artifact people distribute is not what creators reviewed.
current_workaround: Open every export by hand, crop screenshots, or discover a bad label after sharing the file.
incumbents_and_gap: tldraw/Excalidraw own authoring and Playwright can take screenshots, but neither gives creators a small semantic/export comparison report that flags changed text, clipped ink, and missing visible objects.
smallest_useful_product: CLI/browser extension that captures a canvas's accessibility/text tree and bounding boxes before export, compares it to rendered PNG/PDF OCR/layout, and emits an annotated proof image. Non-goals: hosting canvases, editing artwork, or general visual regression SaaS.
success_measure: On a seeded set of 30 export defects, the tool flags at least 25 while producing fewer than three false warnings.
monetization: freemium — a local single-page proof is free; team CI/API checks can fund ongoing browser compatibility.
constraints: All captures stay local by default; OCR must be optional for confidential whiteboards; never bypass application authentication or canvas-origin protections.
why_distinct: It verifies the distributed creative artifact rather than competing with collaborative drawing software.

title: Stroke Lab
user: Digital artists and maintainers of browser/cross-platform drawing tools who need to isolate whether a bad stroke comes from smoothing, device sampling, rendering, or undo history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Pixel-art users compare several editors and report cursor behavior and platform reliability concerns, showing that feel and basic input quality determine tool choice.
A pen-tablet user asks to disable auto-smoothing because delayed strokes and dotted i's break handwriting flow, despite other apps working without delay.

recurrence: Artist feedback spans pixel editors and web whiteboards; even small latency destroys trust because drawing is continuous motor feedback.
current_workaround: Switch apps, toggle an undocumented smoothing setting, screen-record a bad stroke, or submit an issue without timing evidence.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser devtools profile frames and professional tablet diagnostics, but neither provides a creator-readable trace of pointer sample rate, coalescing, smoothing delay, raster delay, and undo cost.
smallest_useful_product: A local web test pad plus embeddable JS probe that records anonymized pointer timing, draws raw versus smoothed traces, and exports a reproducible issue bundle. Non-goals: replacing brush engines, driver installation, or cloud telemetry.
success_measure: A maintainer can classify a supplied bad-stroke report as input, smoothing, render, or history-related in under ten minutes in 80% of pilot cases.
monetization: free — broad integration and transparent diagnostics matter more than gating a frustrating input problem; paid support is possible.
constraints: Never capture drawing content by default; support pen pressure/tilt only with explicit consent; disclose browser timestamp precision limits.
why_distinct: It measures and explains drawing feel; it is not a new canvas editor or a thin AI brush wrapper.

title: Pocket Sprite Pack
user: Game-jam artists working from an iPad/phone or a shared folder who need to inspect, convert, and package small sprites and animations without a desktop editor.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Show HN project specifically converts images into Wplace-compatible pixel art, with commenters responding positively to the need for format-ready pixel assets.
The Android LibreSprite build refuses to load a BMP even though it can open PNG, JPEG, GIF, and ASE files, demonstrating fragile mobile asset intake.

recurrence: Mobile pixel-art conversion and mobile editor-access failures are independent signals; the workaround is especially painful during a game jam or while reviewing shared assets.
current_workaround: Send files to a desktop, use a fragile browser editor, screenshot/crop manually, or ask another teammate to export spritesheets.
incumbents_and_gap: Aseprite, LibreSprite, Piskel, and image converters focus on authoring or one target. None is a touch-first offline inbox for inspecting frames, palette limits, transparency, and engine-ready ZIP output.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that opens PNG/GIF/WebP, previews frames at native scale, crops/pads, quantizes to a chosen palette, and exports spritesheet plus JSON atlas. Non-goals: painting editor, account sync, image generation, or copyrighted asset marketplace.
success_measure: A user packages a 16-frame asset into a valid atlas from a phone in under two minutes, with 95% correct frame boundaries on a supplied test set.
monetization: one-time — a dependable offline utility has direct jam/project value and no reason to collect art uploads.
constraints: Operate entirely on-device; preserve source files; state palette/dithering transforms clearly; test mobile memory limits and iOS download behavior.
why_distinct: It is an asset handoff tool for constrained devices, not a discounted clone of a desktop sprite editor.

title: Gesture Replay Kit
user: Indie game and classroom-toy makers using a webcam as input who need to tune a gesture game from recorded landmark traces without retaining children's or players' video.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer demonstrates controlling PC games with body movements using a webcam and MediaPipe, confirming active demand for body-input experiments.
A MediaPipe user asks for batch Holistic Landmarker video processing and GPU prefetching, because existing tooling cannot process a large amount of motion video quickly enough.

recurrence: A playable body-control prototype and a separate need to process many landmark videos expose the same iteration bottleneck: tuning recognition from raw video is slow and privacy-hostile.
current_workaround: Retest in front of a webcam, keep raw clips, add ad-hoc debug overlays, or write one-off scripts for MediaPipe output.
incumbents_and_gap: MediaPipe extracts landmarks and game engines render the result, but neither offers a small common replay format with confidence/occlusion timelines and deterministic gesture-threshold comparison.
smallest_useful_product: NPM library and local viewer that records only timestamped pose/hand landmarks, replays them at chosen speed, compares gesture rules, and exports a scrubbed fixture. Non-goals: camera surveillance, identity recognition, cloud video storage, or a game engine.
success_measure: Teams can reproduce 90% of reported false-positive/false-negative gestures from a landmark fixture without asking for the original video.
monetization: freemium — open format/viewer builds trust; paid engine adapters and team fixture management can follow.
constraints: Never retain video by default; landmark data may still be biometric and needs consent/deletion controls; no age estimation or face identification.
why_distinct: It makes unusual camera input testable and privacy-preserving rather than creating another gesture-controlled game.

title: Room Ready
user: Hosts of family, classroom, and team party games who need every phone/controller/display on the same local session before guests are waiting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The 121-comment Gaming Couch discussion repeatedly asks for smart-TV support, mixed gamepads and phones, remote play, simple joining, and games appropriate for children and older adults.
Ask HN explicitly seeks a sane casual family co-op game on mobile, showing that finding a usable shared setup remains a current problem.
Discussion of RuneScape's multiplayer design stresses support for weak clients; reliable participation across devices remains a core multiplayer constraint.

recurrence: Multiple independent askers describe the same high-stakes moment: mixed ages and devices make party-game setup fail in front of the group.
current_workaround: Open the game, circulate a QR code, troubleshoot each phone individually, and fall back to one familiar commercial party title.
incumbents_and_gap: Jackbox, AirConsole, and Gaming Couch host games; they do not offer an app-agnostic preflight that tests Wi-Fi reachability, controller/browser capabilities, display casting, and a guest-ready join card.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first web host plus phone join page that runs a capability check, reports mixed-controller compatibility, supports a no-install practice screen, and creates a printable/TV join card. Non-goals: game catalogue, matchmaking, accounts, or voice chat.
success_measure: In observed groups of four to eight, 80% reach a ready state in under five minutes with no host troubleshooting after the first QR scan.
monetization: free — cross-game adoption requires neutrality; a paid white-label embed for venues/training providers is plausible.
constraints: LAN discovery must have a manual code fallback; collect no contact data; provide accessible large-text and reduced-motion test screens; do not claim compatibility for untested games.
why_distinct: It removes the social setup failure before a game begins rather than competing with party-game content.

title: Sim Lab Replay
user: Teachers and independent simulation makers who need to turn an exploratory physics/orbit simulation into a short, shareable experiment that students can replay and explain.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An orbit-simulator Show HN drew substantial discussion, demonstrating appetite for approachable interactive scientific exploration.
Processing maintainers report shader examples rendering incorrectly on high-density displays, showing why educational interactive visuals need a reproducible presentation check.

recurrence: Simulation makers keep shipping standalone explorations while rendering differences make it hard to hand a teacher a reliable, explainable activity.
current_workaround: Share a bare URL and verbal instructions, take screenshots, or prepare a slide deck that loses the interactive evidence.
incumbents_and_gap: PhET provides finished simulations and LMSs handle assignments, but small simulation creators lack a lightweight format for recording parameter changes, expected observations, and replayable checkpoints.
smallest_useful_product: Embeddable JS recorder that captures named controls/events (not student identity), lets authors add prediction/observation prompts, and exports a self-contained replay lesson. Non-goals: physics engine, LMS, grading, or student surveillance.
success_measure: A teacher can create and share a three-step experiment in under 15 minutes, and 75% of students replay the same parameter sequence without help.
monetization: freemium — open embed and local replay drive creator adoption; hosted class collections can be paid.
constraints: No account required for student replay; accessible keyboard control and transcript are mandatory; version event schemas so old lessons remain reproducible.
why_distinct: It packages the reasoning path through a simulation, rather than cloning a simulation library or bolting an LLM onto worksheets.

title: Cuebook
user: Bedroom DJs, VJs, and educators who need to rehearse a music-reactive visual set with reliable cue points, not gamble on a live spectrum visualizer.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker released a high-resolution audio visualization tool, confirming sustained interest in browser-based music visuals.
A developer implementing dynamic compression finds the Web Audio specification ambiguous, a concrete signal that dependable audio-reactive behavior remains technically difficult.

recurrence: Interest in visualizers persists, while low-level Web Audio behavior still creates implementation uncertainty; live users need repeatability more than another effect gallery.
current_workaround: Use MilkDrop/OBS presets, memorize song moments, record a screen rehearsal, or adjust effects live and hope timing holds.
incumbents_and_gap: MilkDrop, Resolume, and browser visualizers offer effect engines; the small unmet layer is a local cue sheet that records beat/time anchors and applies simple parameter changes repeatably across a track.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web cuebook that imports user-owned audio, stores manual time/beat markers, previews a small set of deterministic visual scenes, and exports a cue JSON plus rehearsal video. Non-goals: streaming integration, copyrighted music distribution, live venue control, or AI video.
success_measure: A creator can recreate five marked visual transitions within ±150 ms across two rehearsals of the same track.
monetization: one-time — performers value a private dependable rehearsal tool and should not pay for audio-minute storage.
constraints: Audio stays on device; account for browser audio-clock drift; visual presets must use original/licensed assets only; warn that beat detection is advisory.
why_distinct: It is a rehearsal and timing artifact for existing visual engines, not a generic audio visualizer clone.

title: Patchcard
user: Curious non-musicians and workshop facilitators who make a sound they like in a browser toy and need to save, print, and re-create it without learning a DAW.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Feedback on a toy sound generator asks for local/downloadable output, showing that playful sound experimentation immediately turns into a need to keep and share a result.
A user asks MoviePy for approachable animations and scene transitions, reflecting the wider creator need to turn a small experiment into a presentable artifact.

recurrence: Independent toy-audio and lightweight-media requests converge on artifact preservation: creators want to take a tiny experiment home, not enter a production suite.
current_workaround: Screenshot knobs, screen-record audio, write down settings, or lose the patch on refresh.
incumbents_and_gap: DAW presets are powerful but intimidating and app-specific; toy generators often provide no portable explanation of what was made.
smallest_useful_product: Open JSON patch-card format plus embeddable widget that stores named parameters, a tiny waveform preview, optional local WAV render, QR share, and printable card. Non-goals: synthesizer engine, user accounts, sample marketplace, or social network.
success_measure: At least 80% of cards opened on a second device reproduce the original parameter state exactly, and workshop users create/export two cards in a 30-minute session.
monetization: free — a portable standard needs adoption; paid workshop templates and branded card packs can fund maintenance.
constraints: No hosted audio required; links must not expose private recordings by default; define parameter versioning and clear licensing for embedded samples.
why_distinct: It preserves and explains playful sound settings across toys rather than being another browser synth.

title: Sketch Density Check
user: Creative-coding teachers and artists publishing interactive sketches who need to know whether a work will render and respond correctly on the high-density phone/tablet displays their audience actually uses.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The creative-coding discussion includes newcomers asking which tools to use and calls for more unconstrained browser experimentation, increasing the need for dependable sharing across devices.
An artist reports that drawing, undo, and canvas navigation become severely sluggish even on a tiny 128×128 tilemap, underscoring that creative interaction quality must be tested, not assumed.

recurrence: Creative coders are encouraged to publish interactive work, while artists continue to hit surprising performance failures on seemingly small canvases.
current_workaround: Test on the author’s laptop, add a pixel-ratio guess, or wait for audience bug reports with no reproducible performance context.
incumbents_and_gap: Lighthouse checks web pages and browser devtools profile frames, but neither offers an author-friendly creative-sketch check for canvas resolution, input latency, WebGL fallbacks, and deterministic capture at selected device-pixel ratios.
smallest_useful_product: CLI that runs a sketch through a small local device matrix, records frame-time/input-lag traces and golden frames, then writes a plain-language publish card. Non-goals: remote device farm, source-code generation, analytics tracker, or visual editor.
success_measure: It catches 90% of seeded pixel-density/slow-frame regressions before publishing while completing a three-device local run in under five minutes.
monetization: free — transparent local checks best serve educational creative-coding ecosystems; paid CI/device adapters could follow.
constraints: Run source locally and do not upload sketches; benchmarks must disclose machine/browser variance; support reduced-motion and keyboard interaction checks.
why_distinct: It is a publish-readiness diagnostic for interactive art, not a creative-coding framework or a screenshot test service.
